author: "Chioma Oselu"

## Summary
When we first ran XPASS and XPASS+ on the HPC, the results did not exactly match the
laptop results, even though the run was the same in every way we control. After changing
one setting, the HPC results became exactly identical to the laptop results, character
for character. This note records what happened and why.


## What we checked first
Before looking for unusual explanations, we confirmed the obvious things matched:

  Container image. Docker Hub reports chiomab/xpass:v1.3 as sha256:b845cb81... and that
  is the same image identifier the laptop run recorded. Same image, not a rebuild.

  Input files. All 64 inputs (6 summary statistic files, 58 reference panel files) were
  checksummed on both machines before the run. All identical.

  Command. Character for character the same.

  Threads. Four on both machines.


## What was actually different
The processor. The laptop has an Intel Core i7-7600U. The HPC node has an Intel Xeon
Gold 6248. These chips are from different generations and support different sets of maths
instructions. The Xeon supports a newer, wider set called AVX-512. The laptop does not.


## Why that changes the numbers
XPASS is written in R and does its heavy maths through a library called OpenBLAS. When
OpenBLAS starts, it inspects the processor and picks the fastest routine that processor
supports. On the laptop it picks the AVX2 routine. On the HPC it picks the AVX-512 one.

Both routines compute the same quantity, but they add the numbers up in a different
order, because the wider instruction handles more numbers at once. Computers store
decimals with limited precision and round at every step, so the order of addition can
change the final digit.

An everyday version of the same effect: imagine adding up amounts of money where each
step is rounded to the nearest cent. Adding them one at a time can give a slightly
different total than adding them in pairs first, even though the arithmetic is the same.
The gap is tiny but real, and a checksum notices it, because a checksum reports any
change at all no matter how small.


## How big was the difference
Very small. The two sets of scores agreed to a correlation of 1.000000000000, and the
largest gap for any individual was about 0.000000000000001. One score read
-0.117038894091906 on the laptop and -0.117038894091905 on the HPC. Nothing that could
affect a downstream result.


## The fix
OpenBLAS accepts a setting, OPENBLAS_CORETYPE, that tells it which routine to use instead
of choosing for itself. Setting OPENBLAS_CORETYPE=HASWELL on the HPC makes it use the
same AVX2 routine the laptop uses.

With that setting, three repeat runs of XPASS on the HPC all produced
1732525082a2795a36bd1206437c504c837908fcc20a2c4f9975a00d206ea3fe, exactly the checksum
from both the laptop native run and the laptop Docker run. XPASS+ matched likewise at
fc59d7d126c9da3ab44e6ce5ee457017d5cfe007dfdefa85e44b3733d197c195.


## The cost
Forcing the older routine leaves the newer instructions unused, so the run is slower.
XPASS averaged 86.8 seconds pinned against 78.8 seconds unpinned, about 10 percent.


## A note on xp-blup
XP-BLUP shows the same kind of difference for the same underlying reason, but it cannot
be fixed the same way. XP-BLUP runs GCTA, a self-contained program that does its own
processor check internally and offers no setting to override it. Tracing the pipeline
step by step shows the difference is already present in the very first output, the
genetic relationship matrix. The effect stays small: the fitted variance component reads
0.176559 on the laptop and 0.176560 on the HPC, and the log likelihood and the likelihood
ratio test are identical.


## What this means
Producing byte for byte identical output on a different machine is possible, but only
when the software lets you fix which processor routine it uses. Where it does not, the
results still agree to about fifteen decimal places, far beyond anything that affects a
polygenic score.
